prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of opening ballots I move B036 to the top of my own list, ahead of my opening first choice B017. Optical lattice clocks have the broadest and most robust support on the table: ranked by all eight members, first by two, top three for three, and nobody argues against its scientific standing. The case is clean on the three criteria that matter. The idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping) is original and specific, the achievement (systematic uncertainty and stability at 10^-18, with many-body clock physics from Ye's group) is quantitative and unambiguous, and independent laboratories on three continents now reproduce it with international clock comparisons. It has direct downstream consequences: tests of relativistic time dilation at millimetre-to-centimetre scales, searches for varying constants and dark-matter signals, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap to redefine the second. The credited pair is exactly two people, which avoids the allocation problem that afflicts most other shortlisted entries. As an experimentalist who builds instruments, I judge that controlling lattice light shifts, blackbody and collisional effects to this level is exemplary precision-instrument work, not a mere technique.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit lineage and scope. Frequency combs (Hall and Haensch) were honoured in 2005 and trapped-ion control (Wineland) in 2012, so a prize here must be framed around the lattice concept and its realisation rather than optical timekeeping at large, and ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock groups (PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN) will feel overlooked. Katori and Ye are also not the only decisive names in the strontium lattice story. Timing is a softer issue: the SI second has not yet been redefined, although the discovery stands without it. Finally, my own opening preference for B017 reflects my view that the experimental Higgs discovery remains the single most consequential unrecognised measurement; I give it up as first choice only because no three-person credit for it can be defended against four plausible names and two collaborations of thousands, not because its science is weaker.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B036 first as atomic physics in its purest form, measurement-limited progress with consequences for the definition of the second and fundamental-constant tests, and considers the two-laureate configuration clean and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on the configuration and on maturity, and the measurement-limited framing is one I share as an instrument builder. I would qualify one thing: the prize should not rest on the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision outside our remit. The citation should rest on the concept and on the demonstrated 10^-18 performance. I also disagree mildly with your second choice. Your B046 trio of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller excludes Cirac and Esslinger, and by your own admission that exclusion would be contested, so B046 is a weaker candidate than B036 for attribution reasons even though its science is strong.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock rests on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal realised with strontium by both groups, that control of systematic shifts is exceptional experimental physics, that the two-name credit is clean, and that she sees no competing decisive claim from other groups.
responses.response: I concur on the quality of the systematics work and that the two-name credit is defensible. Where I would be more cautious is your statement that there is no competing decisive claim. The PTB, NIST and SYRTE clocks and the ion-clock programmes are close enough that the citation wording must be tight, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes mean the committee will be asked why this is not an extension of earlier ones. I think the answer, that the lattice concept enabled many-atom interrogation and a new accuracy regime, is sound, but it should be argued explicitly rather than assumed.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B022) first, arguing that a sharp theory prediction followed by a nature-led experimental surprise opened moire quantum matter, and that early recognition in 2026 would still be defensible.
responses.response: I take B022 seriously and place it as my first alternative: the prediction-then-discovery structure is rare and the replication is wide. But I think you underweight the maturity concern that you, Eriksson and Johansson all note yourselves: the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated phases remain unsettled eight years on. You also flag that Cao, the first-author experimentalist, is outside the credited names. A prize that leaves out the person who did the decisive measurement invites a credit controversy that B036 does not. I would revisit B022 in a few years rather than now.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B021) first as a clean invention criterion with overwhelming independent confirmation, and also ranks B036 second.
responses.response: I accept that B021 is a clear invention with decisive impact, and I am sympathetic as an instrument person. But aberration correction is a technique serving other sciences, and I cannot yet see the committee agreeing on its physics weight against a result like the lattice clock, which is itself a physical measurement platform. Since you also rank B036 second and rate its attribution as clean, I would ask whether your first choice has any support beyond your own ballot; only one of eight members placed it in the ranked list.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks jamming and rigidity (B034) first, as a conceptually clean statistical-mechanical account of rigidity in disordered athermal matter, with links to optimisation and learning landscapes.
responses.response: The conceptual unification is real and the two-name credit is neat. My reservation is that the opening evidence for B034 comes essentially from your ballot alone, and your own assessment notes that the relation to glass physics and the universality class remain debated. That is a more open interpretive question than lattice-clock performance, which is measured directly and reproduced. I would need to see another member make the physical case before I could weigh B034 as a prize candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree on a three-person Higgs credit (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee versus Gianotti) in a way that gives B017 a fair path; that is my main unresolved question.

Whether a lattice-clock citation can be drawn tightly enough to distinguish it from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether other lattice-clock groups have decisive priority claims not captured in the credited names.
Whether a two-part prize combining B036 with another achievement could be framed within the three-person limit; I see no clean pairing, because B022, B054, B046 and B044 each need three names.
I rely on my own knowledge of the instrument histories and have not verified spokesperson or priority dates independently.
statement.conflict_note: As chair and an astroparticle experimentalist I have documented ties to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, and a doctoral background through CERN; these are adjacent to B012 (IceCube neutrino astronomy) and B017 (ATLAS and CMS) but no specific personal or institutional connection to any credited person is apparent from my profile. Neither of those ballots is my preferred configuration, and no conflict is apparent for B036.
